submission.natural_language_explanation: This pole is a legal-notice detector: it fires on the stock wording of software licences, copyright notices and terms-of-use statements — 'Permission is hereby granted, free of charge', 'INCLUDING, BUT NOT LIMITED TO', 'WITHOUT WARRANTY OF ANY KIND', 'or (at your option) any later version', 'distributed under the License', 'All rights reserved', 'Terms of use' — with peaks of 1.2-2.9 and a sustained 0.3-0.7 across a whole licence passage (every MIT/BSD/GPL/LGPL/Apache/MPL/CC/Unlicense notice tested peaked at 0.72-2.8). The peak falls below the activity line (0.25 x max = 0.72) when the same legal vocabulary is used out of register ('seats are limited to fifty' 0.21, 'a vegetarian option' 0.00, 'charge the customer' 0.00, 'reserved a table' 0.13, 'still under warranty' 0.44), when the same permissions are reworded in ordinary language (0.14-0.36), and in obligation-style legal prose such as contracts, insurance and privacy policies (0.03-0.62), narrative, encyclopedic, news and technical prose (0.03-0.19) and source code (0.00); a leftover it does not cover is the isolated single-token spike on subword pieces of rare or foreign words ('qu' in 'roqueforti' 1.73, Greek 1.5-2.2, Russian/Arabic/Hindi 1.1-1.3).

rival_explanations: It is a set of trigger tokens rather than a register: ' LIMITED', ' hereby', ' option', ' License', ' reserved' fire the pole wherever they appear, and licence passages merely pack many of them together — this predicts firing on 'seats are limited to fifty', 'a vegetarian option' and 'reserved a table', where the claim predicts silence.

It is a legal/administrative topic detector, so contracts, statutes, court opinions, insurance policies and privacy policies should fire as strongly as licences — this predicts peaks above the activity line on obligation-style legal prose, where the claim predicts 0.03-0.62.

It is a verbatim-boilerplate detector of any repeated template text, so it should also fire on non-legal boilerplate such as cookie banners, README install instructions and release-note templates, which the claim puts below the line.

readings.explanation: This pole is a legal-notice detector: it fires on the stock wording of software licences, copyright notices and terms-of-use statements — 'Permission is hereby granted, free of charge', 'INCLUDING, BUT NOT LIMITED TO', 'WITHOUT WARRANTY OF ANY KIND', 'or (at your option) any later version', 'distributed under the License', 'All rights reserved', 'Terms of use' — with peaks of 1.2-2.9 and a sustained 0.3-0.7 across a whole licence passage (every MIT/BSD/GPL/LGPL/Apache/MPL/CC/Unlicense notice tested peaked at 0.72-2.8). The peak falls below the activity line (0.25 x max = 0.72) when the same legal vocabulary is used out of register ('seats are limited to fifty' 0.21, 'a vegetarian option' 0.00, 'charge the customer' 0.00, 'reserved a table' 0.13, 'still under warranty' 0.44), when the same permissions are reworded in ordinary language (0.14-0.36), and in obligation-style legal prose such as contracts, insurance and privacy policies (0.03-0.62), narrative, encyclopedic, news and technical prose (0.03-0.19) and source code (0.00); a leftover it does not cover is the isolated single-token spike on subword pieces of rare or foreign words ('qu' in 'roqueforti' 1.73, Greek 1.5-2.2, Russian/Arabic/Hindi 1.1-1.3).

It is a set of trigger tokens rather than a register: ' LIMITED', ' hereby', ' option', ' License', ' reserved' fire the pole wherever they appear, and licence passages merely pack many of them together — this predicts firing on 'seats are limited to fifty', 'a vegetarian option' and 'reserved a table', where the claim predicts silence.

It is a legal/administrative topic detector, so contracts, statutes, court opinions, insurance policies and privacy policies should fire as strongly as licences — this predicts peaks above the activity line on obligation-style legal prose, where the claim predicts 0.03-0.62.

It is a verbatim-boilerplate detector of any repeated template text, so it should also fire on non-legal boilerplate such as cookie banners, README install instructions and release-note templates, which the claim puts below the line.
